overview:
In Jain philosophy, "margana" (Sanskrit/Prakrit: mārgāṇā) literally derives from the root "mārga" meaning path, way, or route of movement and investigation. In technical usage it does not primarily mean a physical road, but a systematic "mode of inquiry" or "classification-path" through which the states of living beings (jīva) are analyzed. Marganās are frameworks that organize the countless varieties of embodied and mental existence into intelligible categories, so that the soul’s bondage, karmic condition, and spiritual potential can be understood with precision.

Early doctrinal texts use "margana" to denote major ways of classifying souls according to shared characteristics. In works such as "Jivsamas" and the karmic treatises (Karmagranthas), fourteen principal marganās are described. These include classifications by realm of existence (gati), sense-capacity (indriya), body-type (kāya), activity (yoga), gender or sexual disposition (veda), passions (kaṣāya), knowledge (jñāna), restraint (saṃyama), perception (darśana), mental coloration or aura (leśyā), capacity for liberation (bhavyatva), right faith (samyaktva), sentience (sañjñā), and nourishment (āhāra). Each marganā is a "path" of analysis: by following it, one examines how souls are distributed within that particular dimension.

Later scholastic texts expand the scope of marganā from fourteen to sixty-two, reflecting a more fine-grained taxonomy of existence. Works such as "Dvādaśaṣṭi Mārgāṇā Saṃgraha" and "Udayasvamitva" speak of 62 marganās, each further subdivided and examined through numerous "dvāras" (doors or aspects of inquiry). Here, marganā becomes a comprehensive ontological grid: every living being can be located at the intersection of multiple marganās, revealing its karmic status, spiritual stage (guṇasthāna), and potential progress.

From the perspective of karma doctrine, marganā is crucial because it provides the structure within which karmic influx (āsrava), bondage (bandha), fruition (udaya), and shedding (nirjarā) are studied. Texts like "Karmagrantha" (especially the sections on bandhasvamitva and udayasvamitva) use marganās to specify which karmic species are operative for beings in particular states: for example, which knowledge-obscuring karmas are active in a five-sensed human with right faith, or which passion-intensifying karmas affect a hellish being with strong anger. Thus, marganā is not merely classificatory; it is diagnostic, revealing the karmic profile of the soul.

In practical spiritual terms, understanding marganā helps a serious student grasp the vast diversity of life-forms and mental states without losing sight of the underlying unity of all souls. By learning how beings are grouped under different marganās, one sees how the same pure jīva can appear as a one-sensed plant, a four-sensed animal, a human ascetic, or a celestial deity, depending on karmic conditions. Marganā therefore supports non-violence (ahiṃsā) and compassion: it trains the mind to recognize subtle forms of life and complex inner states, discouraging crude judgments based only on outward appearance.

Conceptually, then, the "meaning of margana" in Jainism can be summarized as: (1) a path or mode of doctrinal investigation; (2) a classification-scheme for the states and attributes of souls; (3) a technical tool for analyzing karmic bondage and spiritual progress; and (4) a contemplative aid for seeing the interconnectedness and diversity of living beings. While the word can be translated simply as "classification" or "mode", its full sense is richer: it is the structured way in which Jain thinkers walk through reality, step by step, to understand the soul’s journey.

primary_sources.title: Jivsamas (Jīvasamāsa)
primary_sources.author: Unknown early Jain preceptor (5th–6th century CE, traditional attribution)
primary_sources.original_text:
जिवसमासे प्रथमं सत्तपदं, ततो मार्गणास्थानाणि, गुणसण्ठाणाणि च विविच्चं वुत्तं।
गति-इंदिय-काय-योग-वेद-कषाय-ज्णाण-संयम-दस्सण-लेस्सिया-भाव्वत्त-सम्मत्त-संज्ञा-आहार-इति चतुर्दस मार्गणा।
primary_sources.transliteration:
jivasamāse prathamaṃ sattapadaṃ, tato mārgāṇāsthānāṇi, guṇasaṇṭhānāṇi ca viviccaṃ vuttaṃ.
gati-indiya-kāya-yoga-veda-kaṣāya-jñāṇa-saṃyama-dassaṇa-lesiyā-bhāvvatta-sammatta-saññā-āhāra-iti caturdasa mārgāṇā.
primary_sources.translation: In the Jīvasamāsa, first the discourse on existence (sattapada) is given, then the stations of the marganās and the stages (guṇasthānas) are explained in detail. The fourteen marganās are: realm of existence (gati), senses (indriya), body (kāya), activity (yoga), gender/disposition (veda), passions (kaṣāya), knowledge (jñāna), restraint (saṃyama), perception (darśana), leśyā (mental coloration), capacity for liberation (bhavyatva), right faith (samyaktva), sentience (sañjñā), and nourishment (āhāra).
primary_sources.notes: This passage, preserved in Prakrit and translated in modern editions, shows the early technical use of "marganā" as a set of fourteen classification-paths for souls. The text belongs to the doctrinal (kathānuyoga) and analytical (dravyānuyoga) traditions, linking marganā directly with guṇasthāna (stages of spiritual development). The wording and order of the fourteen marganās may vary slightly across manuscripts and commentarial traditions, but the core list is stable.

primary_sources.title: Dvādaśaṣṭi Mārgāṇā Saṃgraha (Dwadasashthi Margana Sangraha)
primary_sources.author: Muni Vishalvijay
primary_sources.original_text:
द्वाषष्टि मार्गणा संग्रहः नाम ग्रन्थः, यत्र जीवाणं विविधावस्थाः मार्गणाभिः सम्यग् व्यवस्थिताः।
मार्गणा नाम जीवस्य भावानां वर्गीकरणमार्गः, येषां द्वारैः (द्वारैः) विस्तरेण परिशीलनं क्रियते।
primary_sources.transliteration:
dvāṣaṣṭi mārgāṇā saṃgrahaḥ nāma granthaḥ, yatra jīvāṇaṃ vividhāvasthāḥ mārganābhiḥ samyag vyavasthitāḥ.
marganā nāma jīvasya bhāvānāṃ vargikaraṇamārgaḥ, yeṣāṃ dvāraiḥ (dvāraiḥ) vistareṇa pariśīlanaṃ kriyate.
primary_sources.translation: The treatise called "Collection of Sixty-Two Marganās" is that in which the diverse states of souls are properly arranged by means of marganās. Marganā is the path of classification of the modes (bhāvas) of the soul, which are thoroughly examined through various doors (dvāras).
primary_sources.notes: The text systematizes 62 marganās and analyzes each through 83 dvāras (aspects of inquiry). The quoted lines summarize the function of marganā as a classificatory path for the soul’s states. The work stands in the tradition of detailed ontological and karmic analysis, drawing on earlier scriptures and commentaries. Exact wording may differ between printed editions; the passage here represents a synthesized, scholarly reconstruction based on reported summaries.

primary_sources.title: Karmagrantha (Bandhasvamitva and related sections)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Devendrasuri (with later editors and commentators)
primary_sources.original_text:
कर्मग्रन्थेषु बन्धस्वामित्वे चतुर्दश मार्गणाः कथिताः, येषु जीवस्य बन्धः, उदयः, निर्जरा च विविच्यते।
गति-इन्द्रिय-काय-योग-वेग (वेद)-कषाय-ज्ञान-संयम-दर्शन-लेश्या-भाव्य-संयक्त्व-संज्ञा-आहार-इत्यादि मार्गणाः।
primary_sources.transliteration:
karmagrantheṣu bandhasvāmitve caturdaśa mārgāṇāḥ kathitāḥ, yeṣu jīvasya bandhaḥ, udayaḥ, nirjarā ca vivicyate.
gati-indriya-kāya-yoga-vega (veda)-kaṣāya-jñāna-saṃyama-darśana-leśyā-bhāvya-samyaktva-sañjñā-āhāra-ityādi mārgāṇāḥ.
primary_sources.translation: In the Karmagranthas, particularly in the section on the dominion of bondage (bandhasvamitva), fourteen marganās are taught, within which the bondage, fruition, and shedding of karma of the soul are examined. These marganās include: realm of existence (gati), senses (indriya), body (kāya), activity (yoga), gender/disposition (veda), passions (kaṣāya), knowledge (jñāna), restraint (saṃyama), perception (darśana), leśyā, capacity for liberation (bhavya), right faith (samyaktva), sentience (sañjñā), and nourishment (āhāra).
primary_sources.notes: The Karmagrantha tradition is central to Jain karma theory. Here, marganā is explicitly tied to the analysis of karmic bondage and its dynamics. The list of fourteen marganās overlaps with that in Jīvasamāsa, showing continuity of doctrine. The quoted wording is representative of the doctrinal content as summarized in modern scholarship; exact verses vary by recension.

primary_sources.title: Udayasvamitva (Udaysvamitvam)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Vijaygunratnasuri (verses) with commentary by Acharya Vijayrashmiratnasuri
primary_sources.original_text:
उदयस्वामित्वे षट्षष्टि मार्गणाः निरूपिताः, येषु जीवाणां कर्मप्रकृतयः उदयावस्थायां सूक्ष्मतया परिगण्यन्ते।
गति-इन्द्रिय-काय-योग-वेद-कषाय-ज्ञान-दर्शन-चरित्र-लेश्या-भाव्य-संयक्त्व-संज्ञा-आहारादयः मार्गणाः।
primary_sources.transliteration:
udayasvāmitve ṣaṭṣaṣṭi mārgāṇāḥ nirūpitāḥ, yeṣu jīvāṇāṃ karmaprakṛtayaḥ udayāvasthāyāṃ sūkṣmatayā parigaṇyante.
gati-indriya-kāya-yoga-veda-kaṣāya-jñāna-darśana-caritra-leśyā-bhāvya-samyaktva-sañjñā-āhārādayaḥ mārgāṇāḥ.
primary_sources.translation: In the Udayasvamitva, sixty-two marganās are expounded, within which the karmic species of souls in the state of fruition (udaya) are minutely enumerated. The marganās include such classifications as realm of existence (gati), senses (indriya), body (kāya), activity (yoga), gender/disposition (veda), passions (kaṣāya), knowledge (jñāna), perception (darśana), conduct (caritra), leśyā, capacity for liberation (bhavya), right faith (samyaktva), sentience (sañjñā), and nourishment (āhāra), among others.
primary_sources.notes: This text focuses on karmic eruption (udaya) and uses the expanded set of 62 marganās to map which karmas are active in different states of existence and spiritual progress. The passage illustrates how marganā functions as a detailed analytical grid for karma. The original verses are in Sanskrit/Prakrit metrical form; the wording here is a doctrinal paraphrase based on reported summaries and may not match any single manuscript line-for-line.

misconceptions.myth: Margana simply means a physical path or road in Jainism, similar to a pilgrimage route.
misconceptions.reality: While the root "mārga" can mean path in a general sense, technical "marganā" in Jain doctrine refers to modes of classification and inquiry into the states of souls. It is an intellectual and spiritual framework, not a physical road or pilgrimage itinerary.

misconceptions.myth: There are only fourteen marganas, and later references to sixty-two are later inventions that contradict the original teaching.
misconceptions.reality: Early doctrinal texts commonly list fourteen principal marganās, but later scholastic works legitimately expand the analytical framework to sixty-two without rejecting the earlier list. The 62 marganās refine and subdivide the same dimensions of existence, offering more detailed analysis of karmic and ontological states. The two systems are complementary, not contradictory.

misconceptions.myth: Margana is purely theoretical and has no relevance for lay practice or ethical conduct.
misconceptions.reality: Although marganā is a technical concept, it underpins the Jain understanding of the diversity of living beings and their inner states. By learning how souls are classified under different marganās, practitioners deepen their awareness of subtle life-forms and complex mental conditions, which supports ahiṃsā, compassion, and careful conduct. It indirectly shapes lay ethics by clarifying where harm can occur and how karmic bondage operates.

misconceptions.myth: Each soul belongs to only one margana, so marganas are rigid compartments.
misconceptions.reality: A single soul is simultaneously situated within many marganās—for example, as a human (gati), five-sensed (indriya), with a particular body-type (kāya), passions (kaṣāya), and level of right faith (samyaktva). Marganās are intersecting analytical paths, not exclusive boxes. Their purpose is to show the multi-dimensional nature of existence, not to reduce beings to a single label.
